newsitem.title: USA: House, Senate pass first instalment in budget bill.
newsitem.headline: House, Senate pass first instalment in budget bill.

text.p: The House and Senate Wednesday approved deep cuts in Medicare and Medicaid spending as lawmakers took the first concrete step to implement a massive five-year balanced budget deal with the White House.
The broad legislation passed the Senate by a 73-27 margin and a companion measure cleared the House soon after 270-162.

The mood was cooperative in the Senate, where 21 of the chamber's 45 Democrats voted yes. The tone in the House was sharply partisan, however, as angry Democrats accused Republicans of reneging on major elements of the budget deal.
About three-fourths of House Democrats voted no, ignoring White House pleas for support.
Despite the divisions supporters hailed the vote as a major move toward the first balanced budget in decades.

"The American people are the real winners," said Ohio Republican Representative John Boehner. "By taking this first step toward balancing the budget ... we take a giant step toward restoring their freedom to pursue the American dream."
Republicans will face their own tough disputes in coming weeks as the two chambers work out a final, compromise bill.
The measure cuts Medicare by about $115 billion over five years and reduces Medicaid for the poor by about $14 billion.

In a politically risky effort to bolster the long-term solvency of the programme, the Senate moved to make affluent seniors pay higher Medicare premiums and gradually raise the eligibility age to 67 from the current 65.
The House did not adopt either provision. Despite support from Senate Republican leaders, House Republicans said it was far too early to tell whether the changes would survive.

After a bruising 1996 campaign battle over Medicare, Republicans clearly want a signal from the president. White House officials said President Clinton is not philosophically opposed, but does not want the changes in the budget measure.
The American Association of Retired Persons, the nation's largest seniors' group, has vowed to fight the Senate plan.

"We need to find equitable ways to curb rising health care costs rather than these red meat proposals that endanger Medicare (and) sharpen dissent among the economic classes," AARP Executive Director Horace Deets said in a statement.
Saying Republicans had not kept their bargain to restore welfare cuts and craft a workable children's health plan, many House Democrats who had supported the budget deal voted no.
"It represents a hope and a prayer. It represents a firm maybe. But it's certainly not a promise we will ever have a balanced budget," said Texas Democratic Representative Lloyd Doggett.
White House officials urged Democrats to vote for the legislation, saying they would improve it down the road.
For their part, Republicans accused Democrats of looking for an excuse to vote against painful spending cuts. "I smell a cop out," said New York Republican Representative Gerald Solomon.
The bulk of Medicare cuts in both bills come from trimming payments to managed care, hospitals and other providers.

Seniors would face higher premiums, but would be given new preventive benefits. They could choose from a wider array of health care plans, including a limited programme of tax-free medical savings accounts (MSAs). The House bill would allow 500,000 MSAs, the Senate 100,000.
The administration opposes the accounts, saying they would attract healthier recipients and leave sicker, more expensive seniors in the traditional Medicare programme.
The measures also include $16 billion to expand care to as many as half the nation's 10 million uninsured children.

The Senate measure is more stringent, but both bills would provide states with block grants to design their own health programmes. The Congressional Budget Office estimates the measures will cover only about 500,000 children a year.
Tightening its version, the Senate voted to require children's insurance plans to include a minimum benefits package including hearing and vision services.
In another key change the Senate expanded benefits to legal immigrants slated to lose aid this summer under a welfare law.

In another last-minute change, the House will let states count only cash aid and Food Stamps as income for welfare recipients in workfare programmes. Republicans had wanted to let governors count Medicaid and other benefits in a bid to overturn a White House ruling applying minimum wage laws.

The Senate made single seniors with incomes of more than $50,000 and couples making more than $75,000 pay higher premiums for optional Medicare doctors' coverage. It increased the Medicare eligibility age to 67 from the current 65. The change would be phased in slowly through 2027.
